1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5.strategy: The most testing and most analysed move: the bishop leans on the knight that guards e5, so Black has to watch that pawn, while White develops and prepares to castle. White plays for a lasting pawn centre and a long manoeuvring struggle in which Black has many ways to answer.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once: the d-pawn challenges e5, and after the pawn trade White's pieces get open lines. White gives up the central tension early, so Black can equalise with accurate play, but the game stays lively and avoids the heaviest theory.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop with a target: from c4 it attacks f7, where only the king defends. Easy to play and rich in tactics, it lets White choose between a slow build-up and a quick central strike, but it puts no pressure on the knight that guards e5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c4.name: King's Pawn Game: Dresden Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c4.strategy: A flank move that controls d5, so Black's pieces find less room in the centre. But it puts no pressure on e5 and spends a tempo on a pawn move, so Black develops freely and White has little to show for the unusual set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.g3.name: King's Knight Opening: Konstantinopolsky
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, but from g2 the bishop would see only its own knight on f3, and it could already come out more actively. Nothing presses on e5, so Black can take its time and set up the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2.name: King's Pawn Game: Tayler Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2.strategy: A modest developing move that prepares castling but leaves the bishop passive on e2, where it presses on nothing. Black can develop with a threat against the loose e4 pawn, and White has to spend a move defending it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d3.strategy: Solid but timid: it guards e4 and frees the queen's bishop, but it closes the king's bishop's route to c4 and b5 and passes up any fight for the centre. Black develops at leisure and White gets a cramped, passive game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3.name: Ponziani Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3.background: One of the oldest known openings, discussed in print by 1497. Howard Staunton advocated it in his Chess-Player's Handbook of 1847, and for some decades it was often called Staunton's Opening; today it bears the name of Domenico Lorenzo Ponziani, who analysed it in 1769.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3.strategy: Prepares to build a broad pawn centre, but spends a tempo on a pawn instead of a piece, takes c3 from the queen's knight and leaves White behind in development. Black can strike back in the centre at once, so this is a sharp surprise weapon rather than a main line.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the second knight and guards e4, a solid and symmetrical choice that asks little of Black. It takes the c3 square from the pawn, so White gives up a broad pawn centre built with the c-pawn and usually gets a quiet, often drawish game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.b4.name: King's Pawn Game: Pachman Wing Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.b4.background: Presumably named after Luděk Pachman, the German-Czechoslovak player and author.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn, but Black takes it with the bishop, which develops on the way. White's compensation does not make up for the pawn, so the gambit is unsound.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5.name: Irish Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5.background: The earliest published game with it dates from 1899, played against Harry Nelson Pillsbury in a simultaneous exhibition in Chicago and reported by the Brooklyn Daily Eagle, which called the line the Chicago Gambit. The name Irish Gambit comes from a joke article in the Columbia Chess Chronicle in 1887.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5.strategy: Gives up a knight for a pawn: Black takes it with the knight, and when d4 attacks that knight it simply steps back. White is a whole piece down for one pawn and has nothing to show for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and attacks the e4 pawn at once: White's quiet bishop move does not guard it, so White has to react. Black has a comfortable, natural position and can choose between solid and active set-ups.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once and opens the c8 bishop. If White takes on d5 and Black recaptures with the queen, it will have to move again when the knight attacks it, so Black trades time for quick development; White keeps a slight edge in space and tempo.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 d6.strategy: Backs up e5 with a pawn and opens the c8 bishop: the solid but slightly passive way to meet the quiet bishop move. White can open the centre and keep a small edge in space, while Black has an easy, safe game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: Guards e4 with a pawn and chooses a slow, compact set-up: develop behind the pawn chain, castle and wait for Black to commit. White gives up the initiative in return for a solid, low-risk game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d4.name: King's Pawn Game: Tayler Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d4.background: John Tayler introduced 4.d4 and published analysis of it in Chess, February to March 1981.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: Strikes at e5 at once instead of defending e4, offering a pawn for an open game and a tempo against the knight on f6. An offbeat gambit with real ideas but more risk than the quiet set-up, and Black can simply take the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and defends e4 with a piece, keeping the position open and flexible. The bishop stays modestly placed on e2 and the knight blocks the c-pawn, so White gets a safe, level game with little to hope for from the opening.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre and attacks e4 a second time, so the pawn is attacked twice and guarded once and White must respond at once. Black stakes out space and takes the more active role against White's passive set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d3 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop to its most active square, eyeing f2, and prepares castling. Black builds an active set-up against the modest bishop on e2 and can still claim the centre with the d-pawn later, with an equal, flexible game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d3 Be7.strategy: A modest, safe development that prepares castling and keeps every central pawn move available. The bishop aims at nothing, so White's compact set-up meets no pressure and Black must find the central plan later.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d3 d5 5.Nb.name: King's Pawn Game: Tayler Opening, Inverted Hanham
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d3 d5 5.Nb.background: White's set-up resembles Black's in the Hanham Variation of the Philidor Defence, so the opening is sometimes called the Inverted Hanham.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d3 d5 5.Nb.strategy: Adds a second defender to e4 and develops without blocking the bishop on c1 or the c-pawn. White builds a compact structure and waits for Black to release the central tension, accepting less space in return for solidity.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d3 d5 5.ex.strategy: Releases the central tension at once instead of waiting for Black to do so. The exchange opens lines for both sides and lets Black develop freely, so White swaps the compact, waiting set-up for an open, level game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d3 d5 5.Nc.strategy: Develops the queen's knight to its natural square and adds a second defender to e4. It blocks the c-pawn, so the compact set-up is lost, and Black can pin the knight or release the tension on its own terms; a sound, level choice.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn offered, the natural reply to a central strike: Black is a pawn up and relieves the pressure on e5. White's pawn advance to e5 will hit the knight on f6 with tempo, so Black must keep developing carefully.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d4 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn instead of taking on d4: a solid choice that opens the c8 bishop and leaves White to decide the tension. Black gives up the chance to win a pawn and settles for a safe, roughly equal game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d4 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop and prepares castling without touching the d4 pawn, leaving the tension to White. It declines the extra pawn and the central fight alike, so White can choose between opening the centre and gaining space.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: King's Pawn Game: Tayler Opening, Basman Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..background: Michael Basman took the gambit up and developed it further; this is its critical line.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Hits the knight with a pawn to win time and space for the sacrificed d-pawn. The e5 pawn is both a spearhead and a target, and White must regain the pawn quickly with active play: dynamic compensation and an unclear fight.
Wins the pawn back at once with a developing move and eyes the knight on c6, but leaves e4 undefended: the knight on f6 takes it for free, and White has little to show for the lost pawn.

Develops the queen's knight and guards e4, leaving the d4 pawn for later. White prefers quick development to the immediate recapture, and Black has to look after the d4 pawn, attacked twice and guarded once, while White pays for the pawn with development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5.strategy: Attacks e4 straight away and exploits what c3 cost White: after a trade on d5 the queen cannot be chased by a knight on c3. Black takes the initiative in the centre, and White needs a pin to keep the e5 pawn under pressure.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6.name: Ponziani Opening: Jaenisch Counterattack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6.strategy: The safest reply: Black develops with an attack on the loose e4 pawn, so White has to commit the centre at once. Play can run from quiet and drawish, where White has a little more space, to very sharp.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 f5.name: Ponziani Opening: Ponziani Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 f5.background: Domenico Lorenzo Ponziani introduced the countergambit 3...f5 in 1769.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 f5.strategy: Counterattacks at once with a pawn against e4, but the pawn move loosens Black's own king side. An aggressive surprise weapon that gives White the better game with correct play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nge7.name: Ponziani Opening: Réti Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nge7.strategy: Develops the knight to e7, ready for ...d5 without a knight on f6 for a later e5 to hit with tempo. But it does nothing about e4, and White's hold on the centre gives the better chances.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Be7.name: Ponziani Opening: Romanishin Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Be7.background: Oleg Romanishin tried 3...Be7 in the 1970s, and Batsford's highlighted it as equalising.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Be7.strategy: A passive developing move that ignores the loose e4 pawn and lets White build the pawn centre with no opposition. It was once thought to equalise, but it gives Black no counterplay against the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Qa4.strategy: Pins the c6 knight to the king, leaving the e5 pawn without real protection and threatening to take it. White's pieces come out with tempo, and Black has to find a way to hold e5 and deal with the loose e4 pawn at the same time.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Bb5.name: Ponziani Opening: Spanish Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Bb5.strategy: Pins the knight as well, but does nothing about the loose e4 pawn. Black takes it, and after White takes back on e5 with the knight, the queen move to g5 forks the knight and the g2 pawn, so Black comes out ahead.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5.strategy: Trades off Black's central pawn at once, but the pawn on c3 takes the square from the queen's knight, so White cannot gain a tempo against the recapturing queen. Black develops it to d5 comfortably, and White gets an equal, uncomplicated game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Bb5 dxe4.strategy: Wins the loose pawn. The pinned knight on c6 and the loose e5 pawn look dangerous, but Black has a strong reply to White's capture on e5 and comes out ahead.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Bb5 Bd7.strategy: Breaks the pin at once, so the c6 knight is guarded and free to take on e5. Black chooses solid development over grabbing the pawn on e4 and keeps the central tension, at the price of a slightly passive bishop.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Bb5 f6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn and keeps the centre tension, accepting the pin on the c6 knight. It takes the f6 square from the g8 knight and weakens the e8-h5 diagonal and the e6 square, so Black gets a solid but slightly awkward set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Bb5 dxe4 5.N.strategy: Regains the pawn and piles up on the pinned c6 knight, which only the b-pawn guards, so Black must react at once. Black's queen has strong counterplay, though, and this sharp main try demands accurate play from White.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Bb5 dxe4 5.B.strategy: Gives up the bishop for the knight at once, before Black's queen can attack it. White doubles Black's c-pawns but hands over the bishop pair and the pin, and Black keeps the extra pawn on e4 for the moment: a sound but less direct way to recover the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Bb5 dxe4 5.N.strategy: Hangs the knight: the queen on d8 sees g5 along the diagonal and nothing protects the knight, so Black simply takes it.
Centralises the queen with a double attack on the loose bishop on b5 and the knight on e5. White must find an answer to both threats at once, and Black keeps the initiative.
Counter-attacks the knight on e5, which nothing guards, and the g2 pawn at once, so White has no time to cash in on the pin. Black takes the initiative and stands better.

Guards c6 a second time, so the pin wins nothing: 6.Nxc6 bxc6 leaves Black with doubled c-pawns, but 7.Bxc6+ fails to ...Qxc6. The queen also hits the knight on e5. Black gets a playable game with a weakened pawn structure.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Bb5 dxe4 5.N.name: Ponziani Opening: Spanish Variation, Harrwitz Attack, Nikitin Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Bb5 dxe4 5.N.strategy: Backs up the bishop on b5, which Black's queen attacks, and keeps the knight on c6 pinned to the king. White has won back the pawn it gave up, and Black must now untangle the pinned knight while White's pieces are active.

Takes the knight with check and doubles Black's c-pawns, but gives up the bishop pair, and the knight on e5 is then attacked by the queen with no comfortable retreat, so d4 is needed to hold it. Sound but second-rate: White wins no time and drops the pin.

Takes the knight, but the bishop on b5 is still attacked by the queen and guarded by nothing: 6...Qxb5 takes it, and 7.Nd4 only saves the knight with tempo. White has traded bishop for knight and lost time, while Black's queen is active.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Qa4 f6.name: Ponziani Opening: Steinitz Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Qa4 f6.strategy: Defends e5 directly with a pawn, so no material is lost. It is the soundest answer but an awkward one: the pawn takes f6 from the king's knight and loosens the kingside, and the pinned knight on c6 stays a target for White's pieces.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Qa4 Bd7.name: Ponziani Opening: Caro Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Qa4 Bd7.strategy: Unpins the knight and so defends e5 for the moment, but the bishop blocks the queen's view of d5, so White simply takes the pawn. Black hits the queen with ...Nd4 and threatens doubled pawns, which gives enough play to make it a true gambit.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Qa4 Nf6.name: Ponziani Opening: Leonhardt Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.Qa4 Nf6.strategy: Ignores the threat to e5 and develops, counting on activity: White can win the pawn, but Black gets time to guard d5 twice, bring the bishop out and castle. A real gambit, with compensation in development rather than in any concrete attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 f5 4.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once, the idea behind 3.c3: the pawn on e4 hits f5 and the new pawn on d4 hits e5, which only the knight defends. Black's countergambit has to be justified quickly, while White gets a big centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 f5 4.exf5.strategy: Takes the pawn Black offered and keeps it: 4...e4 attacks the knight, but Nd4 steps aside and White is simply a pawn up. The price is the big centre that 4.d4 aims for, so Black gets time to look for compensation.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 f5 4.d3.strategy: Supports e4 with a pawn and keeps the position safe, but White gives up the central strike that 3.c3 was played for. Black's pawn on f5 keeps e4 under pressure and Black can develop in peace.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 f5 4.d4 d6.strategy: A solid answer: e5 gets a second defender and the c8-bishop is freed to guard f5. But it is passive. Black does not take on e4, and the countergambit loses its sting while White gains space and time in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 f5 4.d4 fxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn and completes the countergambit: Black is a pawn up for the moment. But e5 is attacked twice and guarded only by the knight, so White regains the pawn at once, and the fight that follows is considered to favour White.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 f5 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn that attacks e5 and opens the centre. White recaptures with the c-pawn and keeps a broad pawn centre, while Black's pawn on f5 still presses e4; Black has to justify the loosened kingside with active play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 f5 4.d4 d6 5.d5.name: Ponziani Opening: Ponziani Countergambit, Schmidt Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 f5 4.d4 d6 5.d5.strategy: Gains time by attacking the knight and space in the centre, while the pawn on e4 still bears on f5. Black's pieces are cramped and the knight has to retreat; White has a big, secure centre against a loosened kingside.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 f5 4.d4 d6 5.exf5.strategy: Wins the f-pawn, but the capture takes White's own pawn off e4, so Black's e-pawn can advance with tempo against the knight. White is a pawn up and must keep it with care while Black's pieces come out freely.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 f5 4.d4 d6 5.dxe5.strategy: Gives up the tension in the centre: after the exchange on e5 the queens can come off, and the big pawn centre that 4.d4 was meant to build is gone. It offers Black an easy game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: The point of 3.c3: White challenges e5 at once and ignores the loose pawn on e4, so Black chooses which central pawn to take. Either way White aims to win the pawn back with gain of time, in games that run from quiet to wild.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3.name: Ponziani Opening: Jaenisch Counterattack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: Defends e4 with a modest pawn but gives up the quick d4 push that made 3.c3 worthwhile. The c3 pawn looks misplaced and the light-squared bishop is hemmed in behind the pawns, so Black takes the centre at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Bc4.name: Ponziani Opening: Neumann Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Bc4.background: Jules Arnous de Rivière played it against Gustav Neumann in 1864, and databases use both names for it. Radjabov played it against Anand in 2009, reaching it by the Italian Game move order, and Anand declined the pawn.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Bc4.strategy: Eyes f7 but leaves the pawn on e4 undefended. Black simply takes it, and with c3 occupied White has nothing concrete in return. The best White can do is trade bishop for knight and win the pawn back, when Black still has the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 d5.name: Ponziani Opening: Jaenisch Counterattack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once and attacks e4 a second time, so White needs another defender. White has shut in its own bishop behind the pawns and the c3 pawn looks out of place, while Black develops comfortably.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 Be7.strategy: A quieter set-up: the bishop clears the way for castling and the d-pawn stays flexible. Black does not fight for the centre at once, so White can complete its own set-up undisturbed and hold e4 with a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 d6.strategy: Gives e5 a second guard and frees the c8-bishop, a solid but passive set-up. Black accepts a modest game and leaves the initiative to White.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 d5 5.Nbd.name: Ponziani Opening: Jaenisch Counterattack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 d5 5.Nbd.strategy: The solid reply: it adds a second guard to e4 and develops the knight to d2, the natural square now that c3 is taken. White keeps a compact pawn centre and plays slowly, while Black has the freer game and must find a plan.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 d5 5.Qc2.strategy: Keeps the knight on b1 free and prepares to recapture on e4 with the d-pawn, after which the queen on c2 guards that pawn from behind. The queen comes out early and the king's bishop is still shut in, so White develops slowly.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 d5 5.exd.strategy: Releases the tension at once and gives Black an open game: after ...Nxd5 the black pieces are centralised and White's centre pawn is gone, while the d3 pawn still closes in the king's bishop. Playable, but it hands Black the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4.strategy: Grabs the loose pawn and puts the knight on a square from which it eyes f2. A bishop on c5 would attack that pawn twice, which is why White cannot simply recapture on e5. The main line, with White fighting to win the pawn back safely.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the d-pawn instead of the one on e4. White's natural reply, e5, kicks the knight and rules out the grab on e4; Black must then find a square for the knight in a double-edged fight for the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once instead of capturing. Playable, but White answers with a pin on the c6 knight that makes e5 a target, so Black's centre is under pressure and White keeps the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4 5.d.strategy: Kicks the knight from c6 so that e5 loses its defender and White can win the pawn back. The price is control of c5: the pawn on d4 no longer guards it, so Black may answer with a sharp sacrifice. The traditional main line.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4 5.B.strategy: Attacks the knight on e4 and keeps the pawn on d4, which guards c5 and so rules out ...Bc5 against f2. Black must save the knight, and White then recovers the e5 pawn for an even game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4 5.d.strategy: Takes the pawn back too soon: leaving d4 hands Black the c5 square, and ...Bc5 aims bishop and knight at f2, which only the king guards, so White is driven onto the defensive.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4 5.d.name: Ponziani Opening: Vukovic Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4 5.d.background: Ernst Falkbeer played 5...Bc5 in 1855, and Chigorin first tried the improvement 6...Bxf2+ against Eugen von Schmidt in St Petersburg in 1879. For a century the gambit was thought refuted; 7...Bb6 was revived only in the 2000s. It is also called the Fraser Defence.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4 5.d.strategy: Instead of saving the knight, Black lines up bishop and knight on f2 and sacrifices a piece for pawns and an exposed white king. Very sharp, with exact play needed from both sides and good practical results, but Black has to prove the compensation.
Steps back to safety and lets White regain e5, so material is level. Black can reroute the knight to g6 and keeps a sound structure; White holds a small edge in space in a quiet game.

Retreats the knight to its starting square: White recovers e5 and Black has lost two moves with the knight. Playable, and Black keeps ideas against f2, but it is slower and more passive than saving the knight on e7.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks the pawn on e4 at once, which White's third move left without a defender, so White has to spend a move on it. Black develops with a gain of time against an unusual set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c4 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop to the diagonal that eyes f2 and prepares to castle. Black can leave e4 alone for a move and simply develop against an unusual set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c4 d6.strategy: A solid, modest reply: the pawn supports e5 and opens the c8-bishop. Black accepts a passive set-up and leaves White free to choose when to take the centre with d4.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c4 Nf6 4.Nxe5.name: Dresden Opening: The Goblin
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c4 Nf6 4.Nxe5.strategy: Hangs a piece for a pawn: 4...Nxe5 wins the knight, and 5.d4 only chases it away to a safe square. White has nothing to show for the piece.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c4 Nf6 4.Nc3.strategy: Defends the attacked pawn with a developing move, and with the pawn on c4 the knight bears on d5. White gets a flexible set-up with both centre pawns protected and a fight for d5 ahead.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c4 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: Defends e4 with a pawn, solid and safe, but it shuts in the king's bishop and leaves the queen's knight to develop later. A slower, more passive plan that gives Black an easy game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d3 f5.strategy: A counterattack on e4 that opens the king's side too early. The e5 pawn depends on the knight for its defence, and after exf5 Black is simply a pawn down for a risky attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks e4 at once. The pawn is guarded by d3, so nothing is won yet, but Black keeps every central plan open and answers White's modest third move by simply building the position.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once and challenges e4. White's quiet third move gives no way to punish it, and after an exchange on d5 Black's pieces recapture into an active, comfortable game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d3 f5 4.exf5.name: Latvian Gambit: Clam Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d3 f5 4.exf5.strategy: Wins a pawn. Black's f-pawn has left the king's cover, and the half-open f-file and quick development are all Black has in return. White's solid d3 pawn keeps the position safe while the pieces come out.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d3 f5 4.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move instead of winning the pawn on f5. Sound, but White passes up a free pawn and only keeps the position safe.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d3 f5 4.Nbd2.strategy: Also defends e4, but blocks the c1-bishop and passes up the free pawn on f5. Sound but passive.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5 Nxe5.strategy: Takes the knight, which wins a piece for a pawn: the e5 knight was attacked and White's last move gave it away for nothing. Black can simply take; there is no reason to decline.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5 Qe7.strategy: Attacks the knight a second time and eyes e4, but gives the extra piece back: after Nxc6 the queen takes e4 with check and the material is level. Black passes up a free piece for an early queen sortie.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks e4 but passes up the free knight: after Nxc6 dxc6 White simply keeps the pawn it took, and Black plays on a pawn down for open lines.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5 Nxe5 4.d4.name: King's Pawn Game: Schulze-Müller Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5 Nxe5 4.d4.background: D. T. Phillips used it to beat Harry Nelson Pillsbury in a simultaneous exhibition in Chicago on 7 January 1899. A newspaper report gave the line the name Chicago Gambit, after the city, and some online opening books call it the Schulze-Müller Gambit.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5 Nxe5 4.d4.strategy: The natural try to make something of the gambit: the pawn hits the knight with tempo and takes the centre. White is still a piece down for a pawn, so this limits the damage and hopes Black goes wrong; it does not promise equality.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5 Nxe5 4.f4.strategy: Hits the knight with a pawn but loosens the diagonal to the king: Black replies ...Qh4+ and keeps the extra piece, with the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5 Nxe5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and keeps e4 guarded, but threatens nothing: Black consolidates the extra piece and has an easy game.
